content: The preparation of draft specifications must adhere strictly to the guidelines provided. Clauses should not be omitted, additional clauses should not be inserted, and limits should not be relaxed beyond those specified in the guidelines without consulting Section 4. The material, identified as an emulsifiable powder (CIPAC No. 2), must be dry, free-flowing, devoid of visible extraneous matter and hard lumps, and capable of forming an emulsion upon dilution in water. The active ingredient must pass an identity test, and if its identity remains uncertain, it must also comply with at least one additional test. Analytical methods for the active ingredient must conform to CIPAC or AOAC standards, or equivalent. If these methods are unpublished, full details and validation data must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. Relevant impurities must be included in the specifications, and their analysis methods must be peer-validated. The material must meet specific physical and chemical criteria, such as solubility in water, particle size distribution, and stability under storage conditions. Tests for coarse particles, which could block nozzles or filters, must be conducted using CIPAC standard water D. The mass of the sample used in tests should be specified at the highest rate recommended by the supplier. For water-soluble powders (SP), the formulation must dissolve completely in water to form a true solution of the active ingredient, though it may contain insoluble inert ingredients. The material must be free from visible extraneous matter and hard lumps. Treated seeds must be stored in appropriate containers, protected from excessive temperature and moisture, and users must follow the manufacturer’s recommendations strictly to avoid adverse effects on germination. For water-soluble granules (SG), the formulation must be homogeneous, free-flowing, and nearly dust-free. The active ingredient must be water-soluble, and the granules must pass specific tests for dissolution, stability, and dust generation. The dissolution of the bag containing the granules must also be tested in CIPAC standard water D, following prescribed procedures. In all cases, the influence of treatment on seed germination is critical but not included as a specification clause due to the lack of universally applicable test methods. Users should not treat seeds for which the effect on germination is unknown. Treated seeds should be stored in suitable containers and protected from environmental factors. For formulations intended for seed treatment, a dye or pigment (preferably red) should be included to permanently color the seeds after treatment. In some countries, specific colors may be legally required. The same color should not be used for denaturing seeds intended for livestock feed. Analytical methods for these formulations must also conform to CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards, and any unpublished methods must be submitted with validation data. Sampling and testing procedures for bags containing the formulations must be conducted carefully to avoid altering the sample properties. Bags should be stored in watertight containers if testing is delayed. The dissolution test for the bag material must follow specific guidelines, including the preparation of a stock solution and calculation of the appropriate volume to be added to the test suspension. In summary, all formulations must meet stringent physical, chemical, and performance criteria, with tests conducted under standardized conditions. Analytical methods must be validated, and any deviations from the guidelines must be justified and approved.
